chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: Lateness, CP time and a trumpeter's drinking
summary: Maxwell warns a Black trumpet player at CBS about being exploited by drinking buddies, and Hinton explains the CP-time reputation.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I know -- it's an inside story with the black musicians that we've always -- most of the bands, I don't know whether it went to white bands because I wasn't in any white bands, but black bands, the most famous guy would always come the latest.

I remember years ago seeing Fletcher Henderson's band with Coleman Hawkins in the band, and came -- the first hour the band played without him. And when he came, he was a sensation, absolutely. Well, this might have, in
some sense, put the bad mouth on black musicians as far as studios, because they didn't figure we could make time. We even had an inside experience in CPT --
I just heard it a year ago, after all these years.
George -- Marie St. Louis called me up and told me to be at such and such a place for her (inaudible) and she said, 'that's not CP time.' I said, what's that? (Laughs) I never heard that.
Yeah, we have a little inside joke like that, colored people --

Well, that was the opinion, truthfully, yes. That was the opinion. And I had a long talk with a black trumpet player who was at CBS, and I won't put his name down. And it was about one, his drinking, and the guys would get him out, take him to the bar and drink, and oh, you're a great guy and everything like that. And I was trying to tell him, these guys are not your friends, you know. They're taking you out and they're making a character out of you, they're not treating you respectfully and you're being a sucker. And you're getting a bad reputation and you're showing up late and you're making it tough for all the guys that are going to want to have to follow you. And unfortunately, it was too late, I guess, when I told him. And I think I lost a friend when I told him, but
I meant it in all sincerity.
I bet you did. But it took a whole gamut of black musicians quite a time to live down that little bit of reputation, because people didn't want to take a chance.

And, you know, they were using this guy. There's a wellknown racist trombone player who would tell these terrible black stories. And then he'd always say, well, so and so told me this story, this black musician I'm talking about, like well, that makes the story all right now, because he told it. But it still would be a vicious story. And this guy was suckered. It used to burn me up.
